Below is the summary - please let me know if you have any questions or need any clarification.



*Recommendations*

In order to mitigate Bolt Food's risk of breach of alcohol advertising or promotion ban (see RISK 2 below) and to support 3P in avoiding the risk of breach of selling alcohol to minors (see RISK 1 below), and therefore to proceed with 3P's alcohol store on the platform in PL, we need to ensure that the following features are available in the Bolt Food app:

# *the "age verification" pop-up before entering the 3P alcohol store* - so that the presentation of the offer and marketing actions in the app is restricted to the limited circle of users who are:
## are identifiable (therefore there is no "public" presentation); 
## wish to view such content (therefore deliberately enter the alcohol store);
## are of age (therefore not directing the offer to minors); 

     This age declaration should be tracked and, if challenged, we need to be able to prove that the user has declared their age.

2. *the "age verification checkbox" at the checkout* - so that 3P can be sure that the age verification was done for the purpose of selling alcohol (note that this feature will be required for the sale of energy drinks from 1 January 2024 anyway). 

3. *blurring of the alcohol offer* - for the reasons mentioned in point (a), in the case of partners offering both alcohol and non-alcohol products and presenting the offer only upon the user's age declaration.

*Advanced ID verification* is highly recommended as it also helps to eliminate the risk of false age declarations and therefore ensures that the verification is actually effective. However, at this stage, this is not a blocker to starting to cooperate with 3P alcohol stores if the basic age verification feature is available. The market standard is at least to have the user declaration.

________________________________________________

*Issue*

PL legislation is very strict regarding the sale and promotion/advertising of alcohol and enforcement as well as public perception has become increasingly strict and negative. Bolt Food does not include any safeguards, and the users verification is very limited. 

Therefore, in order to proceed with the 3P cooperation with alcohol stores, we need to ensure safeguards to eliminate or at least mitigate the legal/PR risks.

*Assessment*

The main risks are:

* *RISK 1* - breach of the obligation to sell alcohol only to adults and sober persons in licensed premises - this is mainly the 3P risk;
* *RISK 2* - breach of the prohibition on advertising and promotion of alcohol other than beer or breach of the prohibition on advertising and promotion of beer which is permitted subject to a number of restrictions (the most important of which is that it cannot be targeted at minors) - this risk is shared between Bolt Food (as the platform provider) and 3P - as the owner of the point of sale and therefore the alcohol supplier;
* *RISK 3* - the potential risk of individual couriers delivering alcohol to underage or intoxicated consumers.

To mitigate RISK 1 and RISK 2 - the new features in the app are required (see below); RISK 3 can be mitigated by implementing verification procedures and training for couriers (outside the scope of this ticket).



*RISK 2* - starting with this risk, as this is the main risk for Bolt Food;

* The legal definitions of both advertising as well as promotion are very broad and includes “public forum”:
** *ADVERTISING* is "the *public* dissemination of trademarks of alcoholic beverages or graphic symbols related to them, as well as the names and graphic symbols of entrepreneurs producing alcoholic beverages, which are not different from the names and graphic symbols of alcoholic beverages, *with the purpose of popularising trademarks of alcoholic beverages*; 
** while *PROMOTION* is "*any other forms of public encouragement to purchase alcoholic beverages*". 
* It should be noted that this is a broad definition and the mere presentation of the alcoholic beverages on offer can be considered as promoting or encouraging the purchase of alcoholic beverages (shared risk between Bolt Food and 3P);
* *RECOMMENDATION*: Based on the current state of the law as well as current enforcement by the authorities, it still appears that a restricted access online platform should not be seen as a public forum (i.e. the recipients are limited to those logged into individual personalised accounts of adult users).
* A way to mitigate this risk, and therefore allow the presentation of alcohol offers and marketing activities in the app, is to:
** (i) remove the public nature of the marketing activities in the app; and
** (ii) direct the marketing activity to adults only and only to those who wish to see it.
* For completeness, there are already some case law examples where social media (Instagram) has been established as a public forum and alcohol advertising has been fined there. However, we can argue that there is a difference between social media and online platforms, and to date I have not seen a public example of enforcement against online platforms. Therefore, as long as we are able to ensure safeguards, the promotion and advertising of alcohol in the app should be defensible (especially in the case of beer, in the case of other alcohols the risk will always be higher). Nevertheless, this risk should be monitored. 



*RISK 1*

* Apart from the compliance with the requirement to sell the alcohol in the licensed premises, the main risk for 3P is the breach of obligation to sale of alcohol to adults only. Except for in-person pick-up (if available), 3Ps offering their alcohol products through the Bolt Food platform will not have any safeguards to protect themselves from this risk. 3Ps will have to rely only on the age verification done by the couriers, which might also appear not to be inefficient.
* *RECOMMENDATION:* Therefore, the app should ensure that the age verification feature confirms that the user is an adult. This way, in case of a challenge, the 3P can prove that they have verified that the user is an adult. To this end:
** at a minimum, an age declaration checkbox at checkout;
** ideally, advanced ID verification - ID and selfie check (subject to approval by the Privacy Team) - to ensure the reliability of the verification (eliminating the risk of false age declaration).

The draft of the process (discussed with Emily):

*I. What are Inactive Market tickets?* 

These are tickets that come from areas where Bolt does not operate. 

A ticket is considered from an inactive market when:

# Bolt operates in the country, but not in the city the ticket is coming from;
# Bolt does not operate neither in the country nor in the city the ticket is coming from.

*II. Handling Inactive Market tickets*

# Review the content of the ticket to understand whether it's a Bolt-related issue;
# Ask the user for more details if needed;
# If it's a Bolt-related issue, solve it according to the established process;
# If it's not a Bolt-related issue, advise the user accordingly.

* In order to be able to work on the Inactive Market queue, agents need to have global access to all markets.
* Filtering on Beehive - *_Inactive Market_* in the Tier filter, the rest of the filters should be empty.

I would recommend bringing these points to the business:

# At the start of the NDA it seems that the counterparty expects a local entity to sign the NDA. In Romania Bolt Operations OÜ is the legal entity that signs on behalf of Bolt. They also request too much information as part of NDA, so we should reduce it to this wording:

_Bolt Operations OÜ, incorporated under the laws of Estonia with registration code 14532901, registered office at Vana-Lõuna tn 15, Tallinn 10134, Estonia, duly represented by Ahto Kink in his capacity of Management Board Member, hereinafter referred to as “Bolt”_

Hi Eglė

I apologise for the confusion. All three of the mentioned scenarios have to be met in order for the outbound case to be submitted as _Solved_ without an issue tag. This is based on an analysis by the Supportability team:

* In Delivery, close to 99% of outbounds are *linked cases*, i.e., these are *child cases* created to the original incoming cases
** ±70% of these linked outbounds are tagged as _No issue found in the list_ or left untagged, which gives no context.
** The rest are assigned a user-facing issue, which is essentially is not correct.
* It’s very typical in Delivery that CS needs to reach out to another party to solve an incoming case.
** E.g., call the courier/restaurant if the customer reports a problem.
* On the reporting level, Supportability will associate linked outbounds with the issue titles of the original cases, so there’s no need for CS to do any tagging of such outbound.

Let me know if this clarifies the situation, and sorry for the confusion!

Bina

+*Things to flag*+ 

* I have reviewed the licence agreement attached to the ticket, it is drafted quite vague (it does not go into detail on any of the clauses) however, I understand from the email attached that there is no further agreements or terms of service, and/or house rules (this agreement is the same as the last one Bolt previously signed). 
* The matters I would highlight are: Bolt must be aware that the repairing obligation puts a positive obligation on Bolt to pay for any damage that is made to the *Office Space* as well as the *premises* (the building the office is in). Ideally we would want to narrow this down, so Bolt to only be responsible for any damage caused by Bolt to the Office Space (the room Bolt are occupying) as opposed to the Premises (the whole property). This is because Bolt does not want to be in a situation, where if anything happens to the Premises, which was not the fault of Bolt, Bolt end up responsible for paying damages. *Option 2:* You can proceed at risk, taking into consideration that this is an unmanned office, however you will have to be aware that even though it is an unmanned office Bolt could potentially become liable to damage in the premises.

The main red flag is the repairing obligation I have mentioned above. Ultimately it is up to [~accountid:60420da05290e70069b64add] on how he would like to proceed. Hey [~accountid:6151cf6878e5e40070fb74c2],

I have assessed the Bolt Reward Launch for NL already. 
The following points must be observed:

* There can be *no driver prioritization* based on the performance of the driver on the platform. *Anything that interferes with the dispatch of the rides is strictly prohibited*. If another driver, who rides more on the platform, is preferred, the driver with a lower performance will be disadvantaged, which in the overall context resembles a punishment and obliges the driver to spend more time on the platform. This ultimately results in the driver having precisely no freedom over when and how often he can drive.
* An access to partner offers as a from of reward is fine as far as each rider can join the reward program *at any time*.

Hey [~accountid:5d5ff2f8c6318a0d6cd6ca21] 

Thank you for submitting your request to us.

Your request can be divided into two topics: one being the parking fee, and the other being the user’s alleged statutory right of contract withdrawal. Please see further explanations and my initial assessments below.

*1. The user’s obligation to pay for the parking fee*

Our ’contract’ with a user is principally our terms and conditions (T&Cs). The user accepts the T&Cs on a general level when creating an account to access our services, and then once those services are actually used, specific terms in the T&Cs apply. For example, unlocking an E-vehicle with the user account may be subject to certain responsibilities in the T&Cs, like paying for it and making sure that it’s parked correctly when the trip is done. 

Liability for unlawful parking or failure to comply with Bolt’s parking instructions is regulated by the T&Cs. According to the Swedish T&Cs, the user accepts liability for any parking fee when unlocking the vehicle. If the user has already completed the rental of a vehicle via the Bolt app, the user has accepted liability for any parking fee that may be issued due to the user’s wrongful parking of that vehicle. 

The above means that from a legal perspective, the user would be liable to pay for the parking fee, regardless of whether the user withdraws from or ends the contract with Bolt. However, just because Bolt has the right to claim the parking fee from the user, that doesn’t prevent you from offering a refund to Bolt balance to keep the user happy. This is purely a commercial decision.🙂 

*2. Statutory right to withdraw*

Withdrawal basically means regretting the purchase and getting the money back. Swedish consumer protection law and our T&Cs provide for a withdrawal period of 14 days for purchases of pre-paid passes, provided that the pass is not activated within those 14 days. If the pass is activated during the withdrawal period, the withdrawal period ends and the user can then no longer get a refund because they regret buying the pre-paid pass.

My initial assessment is that the user probably does not have any withdrawal right, as the user seems to have already rented a vehicle under the contract from which the user wishes to withdraw. Renting a vehicle typically ends any right to withdraw that the user may have in relation to Bolt. However, to be able to fully assess this, I would need some further information (please note that I cannot access the content that you have linked in a comment to this ticket): 

* Does the user currently have a pre-paid pass? If yes, is it activated?
* Did the user rent the vehicle in question that was wrongfully parked with a basic pass or a pre-paid pass?
* Did the user write anything else besides what you put in the quote in the ticket description? If yes, please provide the full answer here in the ticket. Please note that I cannot access the content that you linked.

Please return to me with the information requested above, and I will help you figure out how to move forward.

Best regards,

Ida

All the data shared in this process are solely for the purposes to pack and hand over the Goods to Bolt’s couriers and to the end-user - Eaters. This set up is a controller to processor: Bolt gives instructions why we need the personal data and how to process them. 
2. *When this partner is selling its Goods on our platform, not on behalf of Bolt Market, but on behalf of its brand, we rely on General Terms and the Data Sharing Agreement there.* In this case, users conclude separate agreement with this partner and partner doesn’t act on our behalf. In this case, data sharing set up is a controller to controller.
